14G.2 He that touches the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days.
14G.8 Laws concerning contact with dead or unclean things.

precepts.text: Certain men defiled by the dead body of a man could not keep the passover that day; they asked Moses wherefore they were kept back.
precepts.point: The Most High answered through Moses with a second keeping: the man unclean by reason of a dead body, or far off on a journey, keeps the passover the fourteenth day of the second month at even, eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
precepts.why:
“He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days.” There is history on this law. In Numbers 9 “there were certain men, who were defiled by the dead body of a man, that they could not keep the passover on that day.”

They came before Moses and Aaron and said, “We are defiled by the dead body of a man: wherefore are we kept back, that we may not offer an offering of the Lord in his appointed season among the children of Israel?” It was this very statute that kept them back: unclean seven days by a dead body, they could not keep the passover on the appointed day.

precepts.text: The unclean by a dead body or far off on a journey keep the passover the fourteenth day of the second month with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
precepts.point: The Most High answered through Moses with a second keeping: the man unclean by reason of a dead body, or far off on a journey, keeps the passover the fourteenth day of the second month at even, eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.
precepts.why:
Because a man that touches a dead body is unclean seven days, certain men could not keep the passover on its day, and the Most High answered through Moses with a second keeping.

“If any man of you or of your posterity shall be unclean by reason of a dead body, or be in a journey afar off, yet he shall keep the passover unto the Lord. The fourteenth day of the second month at even they shall keep it, and eat it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.”

The man unclean by reason of a dead body, or far off on a journey, still keeps the passover, on the fourteenth day of the second month at even, with unleavened bread and bitter herbs. The uncleanness of Numbers 19:11 does not release him from the passover; it moves him to the second month.

precepts.text: He that touches the dead purifies himself on the third day and on the seventh day; the men of war purified themselves by that law.
precepts.point: Eleazar the priest gave the ordinance: gold, silver, brass, iron, tin, and lead, everything that may abide the fire, goes through the fire and is purified with the water of separation; whatever abides not the fire goes through the water; and on the seventh day they wash their clothes, are clean, and come into the camp.
precepts.why:
The men of war were to “purify both yourselves and your captives on the third day, and on the seventh day.” That is the law of purification: “He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days. He shall purify himself with it on the third day, and on the seventh day he shall be clean: but if he purify not himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean.”

The purifying of the raiment, all that is made of skins, all work of goats’ hair and all things made of wood goes back to the same law of Numbers 19. Then Eleazar gave the ordinance for the spoil: gold, silver, brass, iron, tin and lead, everything that may abide the fire, goes through the fire and is purified with the water of separation; whatever abides not the fire goes through the water; and on the seventh day they washed their clothes, were clean, and came into the camp.

precepts.text: A clean person takes hyssop, dips it in water, and sprinkles it on the unclean; you had to be clean to do this.
precepts.point: Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean; wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. David says this for a reason, because the ordinances set up in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ is our high priest.

note.label: Psalm 51: Acknowledge, Repent, and Be Cleansed

precepts.why:
David says “Purge me with hyssop, and I shall be clean” for a reason. In the law, “a clean person shall take hyssop, and dip it in the water, and sprinkle it upon the tent, and upon all the vessels, and upon the persons that were there, and upon him that touched a bone, or one slain, or one dead, or a grave”. Hyssop dipped in water was sprinkled on the unclean, and you had to be clean to do it.

The ordinances set up in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ is our high priest. So David asking to be purged with hyssop is asking the clean one to sprinkle him and make him clean, so that he is washed and whiter than snow.

precepts.text: The clean person sprinkles the unclean on the third and seventh day, who then washes his clothes and is clean at evening.
precepts.point: Purge me with hyssop and I shall be clean; wash me and I shall be whiter than snow. David says this for a reason, because the ordinances set up in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ is our high priest.

note.label: Psalm 51: Acknowledge, Repent, and Be Cleansed

precepts.why:
“And the clean person shall sprinkle upon the unclean on the third day, and on the seventh day: and on the seventh day he shall purify himself, and wash his clothes, and bathe himself in water, and shall be clean at even.” The clean person sprinkles the unclean on the third day and on the seventh day, and the unclean one washes his clothes and bathes and is clean at evening.

That is the pattern behind “wash me, and I shall be whiter than snow.” The ordinances in the earth are patterned after what goes on in the heavens, and Christ, our high priest, is the clean one. David wanted that purging and washing, to be clean before the Most High.

precepts.text: The law concerning uncleanness by a dead body is laid out in this chapter.
precepts.point: The desire to serve the Most High in sincerity was not there among the remnant of Judah in that time.

note.label: Haggai 2: The Glory of the Latter House

precepts.why:
Haggai was told to “Ask now the priests concerning the law”, and his second question was “If one that is unclean by a dead body touch any of these, shall it be unclean?” The law concerning uncleanness by a dead body is laid out in Numbers 19: “He that toucheth the dead body of any man shall be unclean seven days.”

The priests knew this law and answered rightly, “It shall be unclean.” Holy flesh in the skirt of a garment does not make bread, pottage, wine, oil or meat holy, but the unclean man makes them unclean. Holiness does not spread by contact, but uncleanness does. “So is this people, and so is this nation before me, saith the Lord”: what they offered there was unclean.

precepts.text: Whatsoever the unclean person toucheth shall be unclean.
precepts.point: The desire to serve the Most High in sincerity was not there among the remnant of Judah in that time.

note.label: Haggai 2: The Glory of the Latter House

precepts.why:
“And whatsoever the unclean person toucheth shall be unclean; and the soul that toucheth it shall be unclean until even.” That is the law behind the priests’ answer to Haggai. Holy flesh touching bread, pottage, wine, oil or meat does not make them holy, but one unclean by a dead body touching them makes them unclean. Holiness does not spread by contact, but uncleanness does.

Then the Lord turns it on the people: “So is this people, and so is this nation before me, saith the Lord; and so is every work of their hands; and that which they offer there is unclean.” Like the unclean person, whatever they touched was unclean. The desire to serve the Most High in sincerity was not there among the remnant of Judah in that time.

points: You put the ashes of the heifer in the water and it becomes like a soap, a cleaning agent. That's how you make soap.
Running water: the margin says living waters, symbolizing Christ.

Put in a vessel to wash the person: that's baptism. It wasn't John first. John was of a priest line, the Levites, doing the same thing in the wilderness, dipping them in water, purifying the people. Baptism is not John's creation.
If a man is unclean and doesn't purify himself, he gets killed for doing that.
After the priest burns the red heifer and sprinkles her blood, one that is clean gathers up her ashes; even that clean man must wash his clothes and be unclean until the evening.
This is a statute for ever, unto the children of Israel and unto the stranger that sojourneth among them.

Any man that touches the dead body of any man is unclean seven days. There is history on this law: in Numbers 9 certain men were defiled by a dead body around the passover and could not keep it on that day because of this very statute.

The Most High answered through Moses with a second keeping: the man unclean by reason of a dead body, or far off on a journey, keeps the passover the fourteenth day of the second month at even, eating it with unleavened bread and bitter herbs.

The unclean man purifies himself with the water of separation on the third day and on the seventh day, and then he is clean; if he purifies not himself the third day, then the seventh day he shall not be clean.

Whoever touches the dead and purifies not himself defiles the tabernacle of the Most High, and that soul is cut off from Israel, because the water of separation was not sprinkled upon him; his uncleanness is yet upon him.
This is the law when a man dies in a tent: all that come into the tent and all that is in the tent are unclean seven days, and every open vessel with no covering bound upon it is unclean.

For the unclean person they take of the ashes of the burnt heifer of purification for sin, with running water in a vessel; a clean person dips hyssop in the water and sprinkles the tent, the vessels, and the persons on the third day and on the seventh day, and on the seventh day he washes his clothes, bathes in water, and is clean at even.

Chapter 19 as a whole gives the water of separation, which is the purification for sin: the first half gives the specifics of the sacrifice and what the priest must do, and the rest gives the examples of how a man becomes unclean, whether by sin, by touching the dead, or by being around the dead.
The man that stays unclean and will not purify himself is cut off from among the congregation, because he has defiled the sanctuary of the Lord.
